title: Lecture 4 – Orbit
html:
Source: c4 orbit.pptx – 33 slides

Orbit #1

Diseases #2

  • Can arise from every orbital tissue.
  • the eyeball
  • the surrounding cavities
  • sinuses
  • frontal, sphenoidal, ethmoidal ,maxillary
  • nasal cavities

Symptoms and signs #3

  • Proptosis (exophthalmos),
  • the main sign of orbital diseases.
  • physiological
  • the prominence of the eyeball from the temporal margin of the orbit
  • (12 -20 mm) (14-16 mm average)
  • difference between proeminences of both eyes <2 mm.
  • pathological.
  • the prominence >20mm
  • the difference between eyes> 2 mm

Slide 4 #4

  • The device measures the extraorbital prominence of the eye from the anterior surface of the cornea (dashed line) to the temporal bony rim (F)
  • The examiner (B) views the anterior surface of the cornea through a mirror (C).
  • The extraorbital prominence in mm is then read off the scale (D)
  • To obtain reproducible results, it is important to maintain a constant base setting in mm (E) every time the exophthalmometer is applied.

The exophthalmometer is placed on the lowest point of the temporal zygomatic. #5

  • To avoid parallactic measurement errors, the examiner moves his own eye horizontally until the two integral graduations (black right arrowheads) align in the projection (black left arrow).
  • Once the graduations are aligned, the examiner reads the value of the extraorbital prominence of the anterior surface of the cornea (long white arrow) on the scale (short white arrows).
  • The examiner reads the measurement with only one eye.
  • left eye to read the value for the patient’s right eye and vice versa.

Symptoms and signs #6

  • Motility disturbances of the eye
  • by damaging the extraocular muscles or nerves(3,4,6)
  • Visual disturbances
  • Diminishing the VA by lesions of the optic nerve.
  • Local inflammatory phenomena
  • swelling of the eyelids,
  • chemosis of the bulbar conjunctiva
  • congestion of the veins
  • Local pain

Classification of proptoses #7

  • In systemic diseases
  • in orbital diseases.

Proptoses in systemic diseases #8

  • Characteristics.
  • bilateral.
  • axial (in the direction of longitudinal axis of the orbit)
  • can be reduced with 1-2 mm
  • light pressure applied upon the ocular globe.
  • Etiology
  • thyroid, pituitary and congenital diseases
  • most frequently in Basedow’s disease

Basedow’s disease #9

  • Autoimmune disorder with orbital involvement frequently associated with thyroid dysfunction.
  • Histologic examination reveals inflammatory infiltration of the orbital cavity.
  • Etiology:
  • not clear.
  • Histologic examination reveals lymphocytic infiltration of the orbital cavity.
  • The ocular muscles are particularly severely affected.
  • Fibrosis develops after the acute phase.

Pathophysiology. (Basedow’s disease) #10

  • a) benign form
  • nonprogressive and <3mm.
  • superior eyelid retraction by compression of orbital fat causes the ocular globe to become prominent.

Pathophysiology. (Basedow’s disease) #11

  • b) malign form
  • progressive and very hard to be therapeutically influenced.
  • caused by a pituitary hormone (TSH)
  • exophthalmic component.
  • edema and hypertrophy of orbital fat and extrinsic muscles.
  • increased exophthalmos(25-30 mm);
  • ocular globes (length 25 mm) get out of the orbit
  • the eyelids do not cover the eyeball and close behind the globe;
  • optic nerve stretched may be palpated laterally;
  • ON damages with consequences upon the sight;
  • lagophthalmic keratitis

Typical signs #12

  • exophthalmos, (readily apparent in the left eye)
  • retraction of the upper eyelid with visible sclera superior to the limbus (Dalrymple’s sign),
  • conjunctival injection, and fixed gaze (Kocher’s sign).

Slide 13 #13

  • Clinical diagnosis is supported by thickening of the extraocular muscles identified In ultrasound or CT studies
  • The further diagnostic work-up requires the cooperation of an internist, endocrinologist, and radiologist.
  • thickening of the extraocular muscles in the right orbit, primarily the rectus medialis (1) and rectus lateralis (2), and of the rectus medialis (3) in the left orbit.

Management. #14

  • Protection of ocular globe.
  • Lubricants
  • temporary blepharoraphy until exophthalmos is treated.
  • Actions directed towards orbital tissue.
  • (1) orbital decompression through external wall
  • orbitotomy with removal of a part of the orbital adipose tissue
  • (2) irradiation of the orbital contents
  • (3) local corticotherapy.
  • Actions directed towards pituitary gland.
  • hypophysectomy
  • irradiation

Proptosis in orbital diseases #15

  • Characteristics:
  • mostly unilateral
  • lateral exophthalmos
  • deviation of the globe on the opposite side of the pathological process
  • usually diplopia ;
  • non reductible
  • visual disturbances (ON involvement)
  • ocular movement disturbances (muscle impairment)
  • Etiology.
  • orbital inflammations
  • tumors.

Inflammatory proptoses #16

  • etiopathogenetic
  • a) opened injuries of the orbital margins
  • b) by spreading and inflammatory process from the neighbourhood
  • eyeball, sinuses, face, skin, medium ear, rhinopharinx ,dental lesions
  • c)by spreading an inflammatory process from systemic diseases
  • inflammatory metastases within the orbit
  • influenza, typhoid fever, scarlet fever, tuberculosis, syphilis

Inflammatory proptoses #17

  • classified into four groups:
  • orbital osteoperiostitis
  • (involvement of the osteoperiostal cover of the orbit)
  • orbital cellulites
  • (impairment of the orbital fat contents);
  • tenonites
  • (involvement of the Tenon’s capsule);
  • orbital trombophlebites
  • (impairment of the orbital veins).

Orbital osteoperiostites #18

  • Classification. Symptoms and signs
  • anterior osteoperiostites
  • affect orbital margins in their external portions.
  • swelling of the eyelids, chemosis and local pain

Orbital osteoperiostites #19

  • Classification. Symptoms and signs
  • posterior osteoperiostites
  • sphenoidal fissure syndrome
  • due to osteoperiostitis of the sphenoidal cleft,
  • proptosis,
  • motility disturbances of the eyeball (damages of the 3,4,6 nerves)
  • sensitive disturbances in the distribution area of the ophthalmic division of the 5 nerve)
  • apex orbital syndrome
  • caused by osteoperiostitis of the sphenoidal slit and optic canal
  • signs of the sphenoidal slit syndrome,
  • visual changes due to optic nerve damages.

Orbital osteoperiostites #20

  • Treatment
  • etiological.
  • antibiotic systemically

Orbital celulites #21

  • inflammation of the orbital fat
  • Classification.
  • serous
  • purulent (suppurating form).
  • abscess
  • localized suppuration
  • Phlegmon
  • diffuse suppuration

Orbital celulites #22

  • Symptoms and signs.
  • serous celulitis
  • axial proptosis,
  • aching pain at the ocular movements,
  • visual disturbances,
  • Fever
  • malaise.

Orbital celulites #23

  • Symptoms and signs.
  • abscess
  • a more conspicuous proptosis
  • limitations of the ocular movements towards the abscess
  • diplopia (displacement of the globe interferes with the action of ocular muscles)
  • more striking inflammatory phenomena of the conjunctiva and eyelids
  • general status is bad

Orbital celulites #24

  • Symptoms and signs.
  • phlegmon
  • ocular motility may totally disappear (ophthalmoplegia)
  • infiltration of muscles with pus
  • depression of sight
  • bad general status
  • septic fever

Orbital celulitis #25

  • exophthalmos
  • severe chemosis (conjunctival swelling)
  • eyelid swelling,
  • Significantly limited ocular motility (“cemented” globe)
  • Patients may exhibit
  • leukocytosis
  • increased erythrocyte sedimentation rate.
  • Where there is clinical evidence of involvement of the paranasal sinuses, an ENT specialist should be consulted to evaluate the sinuses and initiate any necessary treatment.

Orbital celulites #26

  • Complications
  • spreading the infection within the eyeball or the cranial cavity
  • meningoencephalic suppurations
  • suppuration of the cavernous sinus.
  • Treatment is etiological.
  • Antibiotics systemically
  • Treatment of underlying sinusitis in applicable cases.
  • Surgical
  • evacuation of pus mandatary if collected

Tenonites #27

  • Tenon’s capsule
  • a fibrous capsule lines the outer sclera
  • Symptoms and signs.
  • serous
  • mild proptosis,
  • aching at ocular movements
  • edema an hyperemia of the pericorneal bulbar conjunctiva.
  • purulent
  • proptosis becomes more conspicuous
  • ocular motility very much impaired.

Tenonites #28

  • Etiology.
  • orbital cellulitis and panophtalmitis
  • most frequently in rheumatism or infectocontagious diseases.
  • Treatment
  • etiological
  • systemically antibiotics,
  • corticosteroids and nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs

Orbital trombophlebites #29

  • Etiology.
  • inflammation of the orbital veins,
  • infection from suppurating processes of the eyelids, nose, upper lip and cheek.
  • Symptoms and signs.
  • swelling of the eyelids with a parchment like appearance
  • dilated and tortuous veins
  • under the skin of the eyelids
  • within the conjunctiva.
  • fever,
  • Headaches
  • malaise

Orbital trombophlebites #30

  • Complications
  • spreading the infection within cranial cavity
  • meningoencephalic suppurations
  • Supurations trombosis of the cavernous sinus,
  • severe acute clinical syndrome in which the spaces of the cavernous sinus posterior to the orbital cavity become thrombosed, usually in the presence of adjacent purulent processes.
  • Treatment
  • etiological,
  • antibiotics systemically .

Tumoral proptoses #31

  • Particularities
  • primary tumors
  • every and each orbital tissues;
  • metastatic tumors
  • the blood, digestive apparatus, prostatic gland;
  • propagated tumor
  • the periorbital sinuses or cranial cavity.
  • unusually,
  • ON tumors (gliomas), limphoreticulosarcomas
  • children
  • epitheliomas ,sarcomas of the orbital tissues
  • adults and elderly.

Tumoral proptoses #32

  • Particularities
  • All orbital tumors displace the globe and cause exophthalmos that is frequently associated with limited ocular motility.

Tumoral proptoses #33

  • Treatment
  • surgery
  • single endocapsulated tumor
  • excizion;
  • diffuse infiltration of the orbit
  • exenteration
  • extirpation of the whole contents of the orbit including the eyeball and orbital periosteum;
  • orbit will be covered with skin above with a prosthesis will be applied.
  • Access to the orbital cavity
  • through an anterior approach (transconjunctival or transpalpebral approaches yield good cosmetic results)
  • through a lateral approach.
